summary:
Our project develops a machine learning-based Earth Analog Discovery and Characterization Platform that identifies terrestrial locations with high relevance to specific Moon and Mars mission objectives. Instead of relying on manually curated lists of analog sites or visual resemblance alone, our model is supposed to be trained on open Earth, Moon, and Mars datasets, including topography, geology, terrain roughness, environmental conditions, mineral signatures, and resource indicators from known planetary analog regions.

The system analyzes similarities between planetary sites of interest and candidate Earth locations, generating mission-specific suitability scores for activities such as rover mobility testing, drilling operations, habitat deployment, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), and scientific exploration. In addition, it explains the trade-offs behind each recommendation by highlighting the most influential environmental and geological factors.

This directly addresses the challenge's problem statement by providing a data-driven method for discovering and characterizing new Earth analog sites rather than simply listing superficially similar landscapes. By combining heterogeneous datasets and machine learning, our platform helps researchers identify better testing environments, reduce mission risk, and improve the selection of terrestrial sites for future lunar and Martian technology validation.
details:
TerraMirror

Finding new Earth test sites for future Moon and Mars missions

Executive Summary | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Team: Analognauts | GitHub: [https://github.com/aisamai63/terramirror]

Future Moon and Mars missions require Earth-based analogue sites for rover testing, habitat development, astronaut training, and mission preparation. Today, researchers rely on a limited number of well-known analogue locations, making discovery slow, manual, and difficult to scale.

TerraMirror helps scientists discover previously overlooked Earth locations that could support future Moon and Mars missions. By combining terrain science with machine learning, it compares planetary terrain against thousands of Earth locations and identifies promising matches supported by transparent evidence.

Rather than relying on fixed catalogues of known sites, TerraMirror expands the search space, helping scientists discover candidate locations that may otherwise remain hidden.

TerraMirror addresses a key bottleneck in planetary exploration: finding suitable testing environments on Earth.

The platform:

  • Reduces years of site scouting into days of evidence-based screening.
  • Supports future NASA missions by identifying promising locations for field testing and mission preparation.

Every candidate site includes supporting evidence such as terrain metrics, neural similarity measures, land-cover information, and data-quality indicators, allowing researchers to understand why a location was recommended.

The current prototype has:

  • Evaluated 3,762 Earth terrain patches
  • Analysed 255 Mars terrain targets
  • Identified 74 unique candidate locations
  • Generated 131 new Top-5 analogue matches
  • Produced 21 new first-ranked analogue discoveries

TerraMirror evaluated 3,762 Earth terrain patches and identified 74 unique candidate analogue locations across seven countries, including 21 new first-ranked Mars analogues.

TerraMirror is currently a discovery platform, not a validation platform.

Key limitations include:

  • Geological validation has not yet been completed.
  • Benchmark performance metrics are still under development.
  • Geological and environmental layers are not yet integrated into the matching process.

TerraMirror transforms analogue site selection from manual search into data-driven discovery. By helping researchers identify Earth’s hidden analogue sites, it could help accelerate humanity's return to the Moon and journey to Mars.
